scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the local `Attachment` datatype definition in the R4 core package with the `Attachment` datatype in the R6 ballot core package. The R6 counterpart is present at the expected canonical URL, id, and type. Findings are limited to local `Attachment` element, binding, type, and semantic-text changes. The R6 base definition changed from `Element` to `DataType`, and inherited `id`/`extension` details differ in the snapshots, but those are base-artifact concerns and are excluded from `findings[]` under the inherited/base-artifact scope rule.
outOfScope: The Attachment baseDefinition change from http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/Element to http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/DataType is a datatype hierarchy/base-artifact issue, not a local Attachment finding.
Inherited changes on Attachment.id and Attachment.extension, including inherited Element/Extension constraints and wording, are excluded.
Global primitive datatype behavior is out of scope except where a local Attachment element explicitly changed type, such as Attachment.size.
Profiles, implementation guides, examples, search parameters, operations, and downstream resources that use Attachment were not assessed except as migration context.

narrativeReportMd:
# Attachment R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`Attachment` keeps the same identity and does not remove or require any existing local element, but it has material migration risks: `Attachment.language` now has a required BCP-47 binding, `Attachment.size` changes from `unsignedInt` to `integer64`, and R6 adds optional media/page metadata that R4 cannot carry without extensions.

## Scope
The report covers local `Attachment` elements and bindings only. The baseDefinition shift from `Element` to `DataType` and inherited `id`/`extension` snapshot changes are excluded and should be handled by base-artifact reports.

## Main migration themes
R4-to-R6 validation is mostly compatible for ordinary instances, except that invalid or non-standard language tags that passed R4's preferred binding can become R6 terminology errors. The largest runtime/codegen issue is `Attachment.size`, where generated models and serializers need a 64-bit representation and should still enforce the domain expectation that byte counts are non-negative. R6-to-R4 conversion is lossy for the new `height`, `width`, `frames`, `duration`, and `pages` elements unless a cross-version extension policy is used.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact local finding is the `size` type change because it affects generated code, numeric range handling, JSON precision choices, and R6-to-R4 representability. The language binding strengthening is the only potential hard instance-validation break found.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most useful for deciding how strictly to validate BCP-47 language tags during migration and how to handle large or negative `integer64` sizes in R6 content. Official rationale and terminology-server expansion behavior would improve confidence.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The new optional metadata fields are R4-to-R6 compatible by design. The `language` binding could have been made less disruptive by keeping a warning-level or extensible-style transition, while the `size` widening appears motivated by real large attachments but would benefit from an explicit non-negative constraint or migration note.

## Follow-up analysis
Analyze `DataType`/`Element` for inherited hierarchy effects and `integer64` for cross-release primitive serialization and range behavior.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Attachment` has no local element removals or requiredness increases, but it has one potential R4-to-R6 validation break (`language`) and significant runtime/round-trip risks around `size` and new optional media metadata. The main uncertainty is how terminology servers and implementers enforce BCP-47 and `integer64` in practice.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration work should focus on three themes: validate or normalize `Attachment.language` to proper BCP-47 tags before R6 validation; update code generators and persistence layers for `Attachment.size` as a 64-bit value while preserving non-negative byte-count semantics; and define an R6-to-R4 extension or loss policy for the new media/page metadata fields. Existing element names, cardinalities, modifier flags, and most summary behavior remain stable.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural differences because both primary StructureDefinitions and package indexes were available locally and the R6 counterpart is unambiguous. Confidence is lower for exact terminology runtime behavior and ballot rationale because no official diff, final migration note, or terminology-server expansion was supplied.

findings.title: Attachment.language binding strengthened from preferred Common Languages to required All Languages

oldState.summary: Optional code with preferred binding to Common Languages.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 also carried a maxValueSet extension to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages`, but the computable base binding strength on `Attachment.language` was `preferred`, so non-Common-Languages values were not required-binding errors.

semanticText.definition: The human language of the content. The value can be any valid value according to BCP 47.
semanticText.requirements: Users need to be able to choose between the languages in a set of attachments.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 treated the common-language list as guidance for `Attachment.language`; base validation did not require the value to come from that ValueSet.

newState.summary: Optional code with required binding to All Languages.

binding.description: IETF language tag for a human language.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 required ValueSet composes all codes from `urn:ietf:bcp:47` and adds `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/languages` as a starter additional binding.

semanticText.definition: The human language of the content. The value can be any valid value according to BCP 47.
semanticText.requirements: Users need to be able to choose between the languages in a set of attachments.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 makes BCP-47 conformance a required terminology condition for `Attachment.language`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are identical in R4 and R6; only the binding strength/valueSet metadata changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 instance with a syntactically valid `code` value that was not a valid BCP-47 tag could pass base R4 validation because the binding was preferred. In R6, the same value is subject to a required binding to all BCP-47 language tags and can become a terminology validation error. Systems that already enforced the R4 definition text or maxValueSet will see little practical change.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect language tags can affect document selection, rendering, accessibility, or patient communication, but the change mainly turns a data-quality issue into a validation failure.

justification.inferredGoal: Make the computable binding match the long-standing definition that Attachment.language is a BCP-47 language tag.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep a weaker or warning-level BCP-47 rule for a transition instead of making the base binding required immediately.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal appears reasonable: the R4 definition already described `Attachment.language` as a BCP-47 value, and R6 makes that computable with a required all-languages binding. The remaining compatibility cost is real because R4's preferred binding allowed some legacy or local codes to pass base validation. A less-breaking transition exists, but it is incomplete for the inferred goal because it keeps invalid language tags acceptable or only warning-level.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have retained a preferred/extensible-style binding or added a best-practice warning for one release while encouraging normalization to valid BCP-47 tags. That would preserve old instances with local or malformed codes, but it would delay consistent validation and leave receivers unable to rely on base R6 terminology conformance.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve more legacy non-BCP-47 values, but it would not deliver uniform machine-checkable BCP-47 conformance in base R6.

evidence.detail: R4 binding strength is preferred and valueSet is http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/languages.
R6 binding strength is required and valueSet is http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4, with Common Languages retained as an additional starter binding.
The All Languages ValueSet includes all codes from urn:ietf:bcp:47.

examples.examplesMd: The example is illustrative: it isolates the `Attachment.language` value rather than a complete resource. A migration should map local/free-text language values to valid BCP-47 tags or remove values that cannot be justified.

findings.narrativeMd: `Attachment.language` changed from a preferred binding to a required binding. This is a potential hard validation break for legacy data that used local language codes, misspellings, or non-BCP-47 tags. Implementers may be surprised because the element cardinality and primitive type did not change, but terminology validation becomes stricter.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: a value that is merely a FHIR `code` but not a valid BCP-47 language tag can move from warning/no required-binding error to an R6 required-binding error. R6-to-R4: a valid R6 BCP-47 tag is still syntactically representable in R4, though older R4 validators may only warn if it is outside the Common Languages starter list.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all `Attachment.language` values, normalize case and subtags to valid BCP-47, and map local codes through a site-specific mapping table. Test migration with common tags, regional tags, private-use tags if allowed by the terminology server, and invalid legacy values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change likely makes the computable rules match the intended semantics. A backward-compatible alternative would have retained a weaker binding and introduced a warning invariant or implementation-guide rule, but that would leave BCP-47 compliance less reliably enforceable.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Exact pass/fail behavior depends on the terminology service's BCP-47 validation. The local ValueSet compose was inspected, but no live expansion/validation was run.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Attachment.language` was a `code` with a preferred binding to Common Languages, but its definition already said the value is a BCP-47 human language tag and the element carried a maxValueSet for all languages. R6 makes the all-languages BCP-47 value set required. A syntactically valid but non-BCP-47 R4 code can therefore become invalid under R6 terminology validation, so this is a real path-level tightening. The affected values are outside the stated R4 semantics, and the R6 change makes that semantic expectation computable rather than changing the meaning of valid language tags.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition Attachment.language: type code, binding strength preferred, valueSet http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/languages, maxValueSet http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages.

R6 StructureDefinition Attachment.language: type code, binding strength required, valueSet http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4, with Common Languages retained as an additional starter binding.
R6 ValueSet/all-languages composes all codes from urn:ietf:bcp:47.
R4 Attachment StructureDefinition standards status is normative with normativeVersion 4.0.0.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status raises the burden for hard validation tightening. Here the burden is largely met because R4 already described the element as BCP-47 and exposed all-languages as the maximum value set; the break mainly rejects values outside that semantic domain.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 instance with a non-BCP-47 code could pass when the binding was only preferred, but R6 required binding can reject it.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have kept the preferred binding or used warning-level/extensible conformance to all-languages, which would preserve more legacy values. Those alternatives do not meet the same base goal of a computable guarantee that Attachment.language is an IETF BCP-47 tag; keeping Common Languages as a starter binding is a reasonable softer authoring aid.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing potential hard break and Medium impact; disagree with treating a less-breaking base design as likely, because the obvious alternatives preserve invalid language tags by weakening the R6 conformance goal.

findings.title: Attachment.size changed from unsignedInt to integer64

semanticText.short: Number of bytes of content (if url provided)
semanticText.definition: The number of bytes of data that make up this attachment (before base64 encoding, if that is done).
semanticText.comment: The number of bytes is redundant if the data is provided as a base64binary, but is useful if the data is provided as a url reference.
semanticText.requirements: Representing the size allows applications to determine whether they should fetch the content automatically in advance, or refuse to fetch it at all.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 constrained `size` through the `unsignedInt` primitive: a non-negative integer, with R6's unsignedInt definition explicitly showing a maximum of 2147483647.

semanticText.short: Number of bytes of content (if url provided)
semanticText.definition: The number of bytes of data that make up this attachment (before base64 encoding, if that is done).
semanticText.comment: The number of bytes is redundant if the data is provided as a base64binary, but is useful if the data is provided as a url reference.
semanticText.requirements: Representing the size allows applications to determine whether they should fetch the content automatically in advance, or refuse to fetch it at all.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 widens the primitive to `integer64`, enabling large attachments beyond the former 32-bit range but also changing generated primitive representations.

facts.note: R4 unsignedInt allows non-negative lexical values.
R6 integer64 is signed and bounded to 64-bit range.
R6's unsignedInt definition documents the 32-bit maximum that R4 Attachment.size moved away from.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are identical, and the only material local content-model change is the primitive type.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Valid R4 `unsignedInt` values should fit in R6 `integer64`, so this is not an R4-to-R6 instance validation break. It is a substantial runtime/codegen change: generated models may move from 32-bit integer/number types to 64-bit long, string-backed, or BigInt representations, and JavaScript/JSON stacks must consider precision. R6 values above 2147483647 cannot be represented in R4 `unsignedInt` without loss or extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Attachment size often drives fetch, storage, and safety checks. Overflow, truncation, sign errors, or precision loss can cause systems to fetch unexpectedly large content or reject valid large attachments.

justification.inferredGoal: Support attachment byte counts larger than the old unsignedInt range.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable as a backward-compatible base-design alternative: existing R4 unsignedInt values remain valid under R6 integer64.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of supporting attachment sizes beyond a 32-bit unsigned range is reasonable, and the type change does not make valid R4 `size` values invalid in R6. It can still be disruptive for generated code, numeric precision, signedness checks, and down-conversion, so `Probably justified` is more appropriate than an unconditional verdict without official rationale.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping `size` as `unsignedInt` and adding a separate large-size extension or parallel element would be a migration/down-conversion strategy, not a necessary alternative for preserving R4-to-R6 instance validity. It would also duplicate the same byte-count fact and risk fragmented support for large attachments across implementations.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The main tradeoff is runtime/codegen and R6-to-R4 range handling, not preservation of R4-valid instances.

evidence.detail: R6 integer64 is a signed 64-bit primitive with minValueInteger64 and maxValueInteger64.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 example value is larger than the R4 unsignedInt 32-bit maximum. The extension URL is illustrative only; a production migration should use an agreed cross-version extension or reject non-representable values.

findings.narrativeMd: `Attachment.size` is no longer an `unsignedInt`; it is now `integer64`. This is likely intended to support large files, but it changes generated type signatures and creates a clear R6-to-R4 round-trip problem for sizes above the old range. Because `integer64` is signed, implementations should not infer that negative byte counts are clinically or technically meaningful even if the primitive can express them.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation should accept existing non-negative R4 values. R6-to-R4 conversion is not always possible: values above the R4 unsignedInt maximum, negative values allowed by the primitive, or values that exceed a runtime's safe numeric precision require rejection, extension, or a lossless string/long representation outside the R4 base element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate models and schemas for R6 and audit any `int`, `uint32`, SQL integer, JSON number, or JavaScript number handling. Store `size` in a 64-bit-safe representation and add application validation that `size >= 0`. For R6-to-R4 export, fail fast or preserve the value in a documented extension when it is outside R4's representable range.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change seems justified for large binary payloads, but a standard large-size extension would have been less disruptive for R4 clients. The tradeoff is that extension-based handling would make large attachments less uniformly supported across R6 implementations.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: No official rationale was available. Human review should confirm whether R6 intends `Attachment.size` to permit only non-negative integer64 values despite the signed primitive.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Attachment.size` and R6 `Attachment.size` keep the same path and cardinality, but the primitive changes from `unsignedInt` to `integer64`. Existing R4 size values remain representable in R6, so this is not an old-valid/new-invalid instance break. The concrete migration burden is generated API, serializer, validator, and storage code that previously treated the property as an unsigned integer and must now handle the R6 integer64 representation and much larger values. The R6 goal is credible because byte counts for referenced attachments can exceed the older integer domain.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition Attachment.size: type unsignedInt, min 0, max 1.
R6 StructureDefinition Attachment.size: type integer64, min 0, max 1.
R6 StructureDefinition integer64: described as a very large whole number, with value range -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807.
Attachment.size requirements say applications use the size to decide whether to fetch content automatically or refuse to fetch it.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status makes the API/type churn important, especially because Attachment is a common datatype. It does not by itself make the change disproportionate because R4 instances migrate forward without becoming structurally invalid.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: generated model types, validation logic, JSON handling, and database columns may need wider integer64 handling; R6-to-R4 values above the R4 unsignedInt domain cannot be represented without loss or policy.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have retained `size` as unsignedInt and added a separate large-size field, or could have used an extension for very large byte counts. That would preserve old generated APIs, but it creates duplicate representations of the same byte count and conflict/precedence rules. Keeping only unsignedInt would fail the large-attachment goal. A non-negative constraint on the integer64 value might better preserve the old byte-count domain, but it would not remove the main codegen/API change.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing assessment that this is not a hard R4-to-R6 instance break but is a meaningful runtime/codegen and reverse-conversion issue; also agree that the available less-breaking designs have material tradeoffs.

findings.title: R6 adds optional media and page metadata elements to Attachment

oldState.summary: R4 Attachment had no local elements for pixel dimensions, frame count, duration, or printed page count.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 systems typically represented these details out of band or in extensions/profiles if needed.

newState.summary: R6 adds five optional local elements: height, width, frames, duration, and pages.

semanticText.definition: Height/width describe image pixels, frames describes multi-frame image/photo content, duration describes audio/video length in seconds, and pages describes printed pages.

newState.narrativeMd: The new fields are optional and non-summary. `height`, `width`, `frames`, and `pages` use `positiveInt`; `duration` uses `decimal`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: These element ids are absent from the R4 Attachment snapshot and differential and present in the R6 Attachment snapshot and differential.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Adding optional elements is not an R4-to-R6 validation break. The risk appears when R6 data is consumed by strict R4 parsers or converted back to R4: the new fields have no base R4 locations and unknown-element rejection or silent dropping can lose clinically or operationally useful rendering metadata.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Most content remains accessible without these fields, but image dimensions, frame count, duration, and page count can affect rendering, viewer choice, bandwidth decisions, and user expectations.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent common media and document metadata directly on Attachment instead of requiring extensions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the new media metadata fields are optional R6 additions and already preserve R4-valid Attachment instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding optional height, width, frames, duration, and pages fields is a reasonable base R6 way to represent common attachment metadata without invalidating existing R4 instances. The compatibility issue is only that R6-native content with these fields cannot be represented in base R4 without loss or extensions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Continuing to rely only on extensions would be more convenient for R4 round-tripping, but it would not be a backward-compatible alternative to a breaking R4-to-R6 change because no such R4-to-R6 break is introduced. It would also make common metadata less discoverable and less consistently implemented in R6.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 export still needs an extension or loss policy, but that is a down-conversion mitigation rather than a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R4 Attachment snapshot does not contain Attachment.height, Attachment.width, Attachment.frames, Attachment.duration, or Attachment.pages.
R6 adds optional elements for media dimensions, frame count, duration, and printed page count.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is validly shaped for R6 Attachment metadata but cannot be represented in base R4 Attachment without extensions or loss.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds direct metadata for images, video/audio, multi-frame content, and printed documents. This is not a breaking change for R4 data moving forward, because every added element is optional. It is a round-trip and strict-parser issue for R6 content moving back to R4.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: existing R4 instances remain valid with these fields absent. R6-to-R4: strict R4 validators will reject these unknown elements if they appear, and lossy converters that drop them can change rendering or selection behavior.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-native systems, add generated properties and tests for the new metadata. For R6-to-R4 export, define a standard extension mapping or explicitly document that the metadata is dropped. Test strict R4 parser behavior with each new field present.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The optional additions are a backward-compatible R4-to-R6 design. The unavoidable compatibility cost is for down-conversion; a cross-version extension strategy can mitigate but not eliminate that cost.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds optional Attachment media metadata fields for dimensions, frame count, duration, and page count. R4 instances do not need any new element and remain valid with respect to this change. Strict R4 consumers or R6-to-R4 converters can lose these new fields, but that is expected for additive R6 data and does not indicate an R4-to-R6 compatibility problem at this path.
keyEvidence: R4 Attachment snapshot has no Attachment.height, Attachment.width, Attachment.frames, Attachment.duration, or Attachment.pages elements.
R6 Attachment snapshot adds Attachment.height, Attachment.width, Attachment.frames, Attachment.duration, and Attachment.pages, all with min 0 and max 1.
R6 Attachment.frames definition says applications should not assume a single frame unless explicitly stated, indicating useful rendering metadata rather than required core content.
R4 Attachment StructureDefinition standards status is normative with normativeVersion 4.0.0.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status warrants checking the additive change carefully, but it does not raise optional new R6 fields into a forward compatibility break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: optional R6-only metadata has no base R4 slot and may be dropped or rejected by strict R4 tooling; there is no R4-to-R6 old-valid/new-invalid mechanism.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base design is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility because optional addition is already the compatibility-preserving pattern. Using only extensions would reduce base computability for common rendering metadata without preserving any additional R4 instance shape.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that reverse conversion can lose useful metadata, but disagree with treating this as a Medium R4-to-R6 compatibility concern; the path-level forward change is additive.

findings.title: Attachment.url semantics now explicitly allow Bundle-local resolution

oldState.summary: R4 described relative URLs as interpreted relative to the service URL, with cid: and transient locations noted.

semanticText.comment: If both data and url are provided, the url SHALL point to the same content as the data contains. Urls may be relative references or may reference transient locations such as a wrapping envelope using cid: though this has ramifications for using signatures. Relative URLs are interpreted relative to the service url, like a resource reference, rather than relative to the resource itself. If a URL is provided, it SHALL resolve to actual data.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 emphasized service-URL resolution for relative URLs.

newState.summary: R6 keeps the same type and cardinality but adds Bundle-local URI resolution language.

semanticText.comment: If both data and url are provided, the url SHALL point to the same content as the data contains. Urls may be relative references or may reference transient locations such as a wrapping envelope using cid: though this has ramifications for using signatures. Relative URLs are interpreted relative to the service url, like a resource reference, rather than relative to the resource itself. Urls may also be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment type. If a URL is provided, it SHALL resolve to actual data.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 explicitly permits URI resolution that only makes sense within a containing Bundle.

facts.oldValue: Relative URLs are interpreted relative to the service url...
facts.newValue: Urls may also be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment type.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The path, type, cardinality, and flags are unchanged; only the local comment text changed materially.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a schema validation break: the element remains `url` 0..1. The risk is behavioral. An R6 producer can rely on a Bundle-local URI that an R4 consumer interprets as service-relative or attempts to dereference outside the Bundle, making the attachment inaccessible even though the JSON shape is acceptable.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: If the attachment is a clinical document or image, failed resolution can affect availability of supporting information.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify valid packaging patterns for attachments carried with other resources in Bundles.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the URL element shape and old R4-valid values are preserved; the issue is R6-to-R4 or R4-era runtime interpretation.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of documenting Bundle-local attachment resolution is reasonable, and the change does not create an old-valid/new-invalid pattern for `Attachment.url`. The risk is behavioral: R6 producers may rely on Bundle context that older consumers do not use. Without official rationale, `Probably justified` better reflects the evidence than a stronger verdict.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A profile- or implementation-guide-only rule could localize Bundle-local resolution for specific exchanges, but that is not a base-design alternative needed to preserve R4 instances. It would trade lower surprise for R4-era dereferencing logic against weaker discoverability and less uniform handling in R6.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping Bundle-local resolution only in profiles would reduce surprise for older consumers but would make a common packaging rule less visible in base R6.

evidence.detail: R4 comment says relative URLs are interpreted relative to the service URL and does not mention Bundle-only resolution.
R6 comment adds that URLs may be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment type.
evidence.quote: Urls may also be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment type.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is syntactically representable in R4, but if the URI is intended to resolve only to another Bundle entry, an R4 consumer using service-relative resolution may fail or retrieve the wrong target.

findings.narrativeMd: `Attachment.url` gained explicit Bundle-local resolution semantics. The local datatype shape did not change, but the permitted operational interpretation did. This matters for packaged documents and images where the bytes are included elsewhere in a Bundle rather than dereferenceable from the server base.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no old-valid/new-invalid pattern. The compatibility issue is still-valid-but-behaviorally-different: R6 content may depend on Bundle context for resolution, while R4-era code may treat the same string as service-relative or externally dereferenceable.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When exchanging R6 Attachments with R4 systems, avoid Bundle-local-only URLs unless the receiver explicitly supports them. If down-converting, rewrite URLs to R4-compatible resolvable locations, inline `data` when appropriate, or include clear Bundle resolution instructions in an implementation agreement.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is a clarification/semantic expansion rather than a structural break. It could have been isolated to profiles, but putting it in the base comment makes a common Bundle packaging pattern visible to all R6 implementations.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The `Attachment.url` type and cardinality are unchanged. R6 adds prose saying URLs may also be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment. That broadens documented resolution behavior for new R6 data; it does not make R4 service-relative or absolute URLs invalid. An R4-only consumer may fail to resolve a new bundle-local URI, but that is a reverse/inter-version consumption issue rather than a break for R4 instances migrating to R6.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition Attachment.url: type url, min 0, max 1, comment says relative URLs are interpreted relative to the service URL and must resolve to actual data.
R6 StructureDefinition Attachment.url: type url, min 0, max 1, same basic comment plus 'Urls may also be URIs only resolvable within a Bundle containing the resource with the attachment type.'
No computable cardinality, type, binding, or invariant change was found for Attachment.url.
R4 Attachment StructureDefinition standards status is normative with normativeVersion 4.0.0.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status makes semantic changes worth checking, but the actual mechanism is documentation-level broadening with no old-valid/new-invalid validation effect.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: R6 documents an additional Bundle-local resolution mode; R4 payloads and the wire type remain valid.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A separate element for Bundle-local attachment references would be more disruptive and would duplicate URL semantics. Keeping the R4 prose unchanged would avoid reverse-consumer surprise but would also fail to document an intended R6 resolution mode. The current prose addition is already a low-breaking design.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that R4 consumers of new R6 data may not understand Bundle-local URIs, but disagree with the existing Medium compatibility impact for an R4-to-R6 review because the change is not a base validation or API break.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, status, and abstract flag are stable. The baseDefinition shift is real but excluded as a base datatype hierarchy issue.
No existing local Attachment element increased minimum cardinality or decreased maximum cardinality. All new elements are optional.
Existing local element types are unchanged except `Attachment.size`, which is reported separately. Added element types are reported in the media metadata finding.
`Attachment.contentType` remains a required binding to the MIME type ValueSet, whose compose still includes all BCP-13 codes. `Attachment.language` is reported separately.

The local `att-1` invariant remains `data.empty() or contentType.exists()` with error severity. R6 adds condition cross-references to `contentType` and `data`, but the validation rule itself is unchanged.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value was found on local Attachment elements in either release.
No local Attachment element is a modifier in either release, and no modifier reason was introduced locally.
Summary flags on existing local elements are stable. The newly added R6 media/page metadata elements are non-summary.
No local Attachment-specific slicing was introduced or changed. Inherited extension slicing is out of scope.
No local maxLength, regex, fixed, or pattern limits changed except through the primitive type replacement on `Attachment.size`, which is reported separately.
Existing local JSON/XML element names are unchanged. Serialization risk is limited to added R6 fields and the `integer64` representation for `Attachment.size`, both covered in findings.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: contentType binding retargeted to the R6 Mime Types ValueSet version
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Attachment.contentType` remains `code` 0..1 with required binding to the MIME type ValueSet, and both R4 and R6 `ValueSet/mimetypes` compose all codes from `urn:ietf:bcp:13`. The binding description changed wording but not the apparent domain.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology validators should use the R6 versioned ValueSet in R6 validation, but no local R4-to-R6 value-domain narrowing was found.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: title comment now notes it may be derived from the source filename
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Attachment.title` keeps the same path, cardinality, type, summary flag, and translatable extension. The new comment is guidance, not a validation constraint.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Display logic may use this as a hint, but migration does not need to populate or transform `title` solely because of this comment.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Artifact metadata and workgroup details changed without changing local identity
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 changes publisher/contact metadata and adds type-characteristics/workgroup extensions, while the canonical URL, id, type, kind, active status, and non-abstract flag remain stable.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Tooling that displays governance metadata may show different publisher/workgroup information, but instance validation is unaffected.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 `Attachment` specializes `DataType` instead of `Element`. Per scope rules this hierarchy change should be assessed in the base datatype report, not duplicated here.
`Attachment.size` now depends on `integer64`; cross-artifact reducers should align primitive serialization, precision, signedness, and R4 conversion guidance.
The `Attachment.language` impact depends on required BCP-47 terminology validation behavior and terminology-server support.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 datatype diff, ballot change note, or Jira rationale was available locally, so justification analysis is inferred from the computable definitions.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Use official HL7 change notes or approved Jira issues explaining the Attachment changes.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The language and MIME type analysis used local ValueSet compose definitions, not live terminology-server expansion or validation of representative BCP-47/BCP-13 strings.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run both R4 and R6 terminology validation for common, regional, private-use, and invalid language tags.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The new input is an R6 ballot build, not a final published release, so details may change before final publication.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Repeat the comparison against the final R6 package when available.
